title: Quantities in Chemical Reactions
seo_title: Grade 11 Chemistry (SCH3U): Quantities in Chemical Reactions Worksheets (Ontario)
standard_text: The mole and Avogadro's number; molar mass; converting between mass, moles and number of particles; percentage composition; empirical and molecular formulas; mole ratios in balanced equations; limiting reagent; theoretical and percentage yield. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 11 and 12: Science (2008), Chemistry, Grade 11, University Preparation (SCH3U), Strand D: Quantities in Chemical Reactions)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Chemistry (SCH3U) worksheets on quantities in chemical reactions: the mole, molar mass, percentage composition, empirical formulas, stoichiometry, limiting reagent and percentage yield. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: n = m ÷ M: change grams to moles before using the equation.
body_html:
How to think about it

A mole is 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The molar mass M (g/mol) is the mass of one mole, found by adding the atomic masses. Use n = m ÷ M to change grams to moles and N = n × NA for particles.

In stoichiometry, change the given quantity to moles, use the mole ratio from the balanced equation, then change to the unit you want. The limiting reagent is the reactant that runs out first; it decides the theoretical yield. Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100%.

Example

How many moles are in 36.0 g of water (M = 18.0 g/mol)?

n = 36.0 ÷ 18.0

Answer: 2.00 mol

Example

2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. How many moles of water form from 3.0 mol of O₂?

Ratio H₂O : O₂ = 2 : 1

Answer: 6.0 mol

Common mistakes

  • Using grams in the mole ratio instead of moles.
  • Choosing the reactant with the smaller mass as the limiting reagent.
  • Forgetting to multiply by the subscript when finding molar mass (H₂O has two H).

faq.a: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound, such as CH₂O for glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆).

faq.q: Why is the actual yield usually less than the theoretical yield?
faq.a: Some product is lost, side reactions happen or the reaction does not go to completion.

items.e: Each formula has 6 atoms, so 0.5 × 6 = 3 mol.

items.q: How many particles (molecules or formula units) are in 0.5 mol of sodium chloride (NaCl)?
How many particles (molecules or formula units) are in 5 mol of sodium hydroxide (NaOH)?
Which quantity changes with temperature: molarity or molality?
items.e: Volume changes with temperature; mass does not.

items.q: How many moles of O atoms are in 1 mol of calcium carbonate (CaCO<sub>3</sub>)?
items.e: Each formula has 3 O, so 1 × 3 = 3 mol.

What is one atomic mass unit (u)?
c: the mass of a hydrogen atom
one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
the mass of a proton exactly

items.q: How many moles are in 500 g of calcium carbonate (CaCO<sub>3</sub>)? (Molar mass = 100 g/mol)
What is the mass of 0.25 mol of oxygen gas (O<sub>2</sub>)? (Molar mass = 32 g/mol)
How many moles are in 900 g of glucose (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>)? (Molar mass = 180 g/mol)
What is the mass of 0.75 mol of glucose (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>)? (Molar mass = 180 g/mol)
How many moles are in 128 g of oxygen gas (O<sub>2</sub>)? (Molar mass = 32 g/mol)
What is the mass of 0.2 mol of carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>)? (Molar mass = 44 g/mol)

What is the molar mass of sodium chloride (NaCl)? (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)

What is the molar mass of iron(III) oxide (Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>)? (O = 16, Fe = 56)
What is the molar mass of ethanol (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O)? (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)

What is the mass of 0.1 mol of propane (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>)? (Molar mass = 44 g/mol)
What is the molar mass of carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>)? (C = 12, O = 16)
How many moles are in 72 g of water (H<sub>2</sub>O)? (Molar mass = 18 g/mol)
What percent of the mass of sucrose (C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>O<sub>11</sub>) is O? (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16; molar mass = 342 g/mol)
What percent of the mass of aluminum oxide (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) is Al? (O = 16, Al = 27; molar mass = 102 g/mol)
A compound contains 25.6 g of Cu, 3.2 g of O. What is its empirical formula? (Ar: Cu = 64, O = 16)
items.e: Divide each mass (or %) by Ar, then divide by the smallest number to get the simplest whole-number ratio: Cu₂O.

items.q: A compound contains 2.8 g of N, 6.4 g of O. What is its empirical formula? (Ar: N = 14, O = 16)
items.e: Divide each mass (or %) by Ar, then divide by the smallest number to get the simplest whole-number ratio: NO₂.

items.q: What percent of the mass of calcium chloride (CaCl<sub>2</sub>) is Ca? (Cl = 35.5, Ca = 40; molar mass = 111 g/mol)
A compound contains C 24.3%, H 4.00%, Cl 71.7% by mass. What is its empirical formula?
items.e: Divide each % by A<sub>r</sub>, then divide by the smallest: C 2.02, H 4.00, Cl 2.02.

items.q: A compound contains 52.9% Al, 47.1% O by mass. What is its empirical formula? (Ar: Al = 27, O = 16)
items.e: Divide each mass (or %) by Ar, then divide by the smallest number to get the simplest whole-number ratio: Al₂O₃.

items.q: A compound contains 2.4 g of C, 0.2 g of H. What is its empirical formula? (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
items.e: Divide each mass (or %) by Ar, then divide by the smallest number to get the simplest whole-number ratio: CH.

items.q: Calculate the molar mass (in g mol⁻¹) of CH<sub>4</sub>.
What percent of the mass of carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>) is C? (C = 12, O = 16; molar mass = 44 g/mol)
Calculate the molar mass (in g mol⁻¹) of CH<sub>3</sub>COOH.
What percent of the mass of nitric acid (HNO<sub>3</sub>) is O? (H = 1, N = 14, O = 16; molar mass = 63 g/mol)
What percent of the mass of glucose (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>) is C? (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16; molar mass = 180 g/mol)

A compound contains 80.0% C, 20.0% H by mass. What is its empirical formula? (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
items.e: Divide each mass (or %) by Ar, then divide by the smallest number to get the simplest whole-number ratio: CH₃.

items.q: A compound contains Al 52.9%, O 47.1% by mass. What is its empirical formula?
items.e: Divide each % by A<sub>r</sub>, then divide by the smallest: Al 1.96, O 2.94.

items.q: Calculate the molar mass (in g mol⁻¹) of C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>.
A compound contains 70.0% Fe, 30.0% O by mass. What is its empirical formula? (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16)
items.e: Divide each mass (or %) by Ar, then divide by the smallest number to get the simplest whole-number ratio: Fe₂O₃.

items.q: A compound contains 75.0% C, 25.0% H by mass. What is its empirical formula? (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
items.e: Divide each mass (or %) by Ar, then divide by the smallest number to get the simplest whole-number ratio: CH₄.

items.q: When hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub>. What mass of H<sub>2</sub>O form along with 96 g of O<sub>2</sub>? (O<sub>2</sub> = 32 g/mol, H<sub>2</sub>O = 18 g/mol)
When aluminum reacts with oxygen: 4Al + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>. How many moles of Al are needed to make 6 mol of Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 6 mol Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> × (4 mol Al ÷ 2 mol Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) = 12 mol.

items.q: When iron rusts: 4Fe + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>. How many moles of Fe are needed to make 0.5 mol of Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 0.5 mol Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> × (4 mol Fe ÷ 2 mol Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) = 1 mol.

items.q: When magnesium burns: 2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO. What is the mole ratio of MgO to O<sub>2</sub>?
When magnesium reacts with acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>. What is the mole ratio of HCl to Mg?

When hydrogen burns in oxygen: 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O. What mass of O<sub>2</sub> is needed to make 54 g of H<sub>2</sub>O? (H<sub>2</sub>O = 18 g/mol, O<sub>2</sub> = 32 g/mol)
When sulfur dioxide is oxidized: 2SO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2SO<sub>3</sub>. What is the mole ratio of O<sub>2</sub> to SO<sub>3</sub>?
When propane burns in a grill: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O. How many moles of CO<sub>2</sub> form from 10 mol of O<sub>2</sub>?
items.e: 10 mol O<sub>2</sub> × (3 mol CO<sub>2</sub> ÷ 5 mol O<sub>2</sub>) = 6 mol.

items.q: When aluminum reacts with acid: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>. What mass of Al is needed to make 0.2 g of H<sub>2</sub>? (H<sub>2</sub> = 2 g/mol, Al = 27 g/mol)
When propane burns in a grill: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the mole ratio of O<sub>2</sub> to H<sub>2</sub>O?
When hydrogen burns in oxygen: 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the mole ratio of O<sub>2</sub> to H<sub>2</sub>O?
When iron rusts: 4Fe + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>. How many moles of Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> form from 6 mol of Fe?
items.e: 6 mol Fe × (2 mol Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> ÷ 4 mol Fe) = 3 mol.

items.q: When ammonia is made from nitrogen and hydrogen: N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>. How many moles of H<sub>2</sub> are needed to make 10 mol of NH<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 10 mol NH<sub>3</sub> × (3 mol H<sub>2</sub> ÷ 2 mol NH<sub>3</sub>) = 15 mol.

items.q: When an acid is neutralized: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2NaOH → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the mole ratio of NaOH to H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
When iron is made in a blast furnace: Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO<sub>2</sub>. How many moles of Fe form from 1.5 mol of CO?
items.e: 1.5 mol CO × (2 mol Fe ÷ 3 mol CO) = 1 mol.

items.q: When ammonia is made from nitrogen and hydrogen: N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>. What is the mole ratio of NH<sub>3</sub> to N<sub>2</sub>?
When hydrogen burns in oxygen: 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the mole ratio of O<sub>2</sub> to H<sub>2</sub>?
When potassium chlorate decomposes: 2KClO<sub>3</sub> → 2KCl + 3O<sub>2</sub>. How many moles of O<sub>2</sub> form along with 6 mol of KCl?
items.e: 6 mol KCl × (3 mol O<sub>2</sub> ÷ 2 mol KCl) = 9 mol.

items.q: When propane burns in a grill: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the mole ratio of CO<sub>2</sub> to O<sub>2</sub>?
When hydrogen burns in oxygen: 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the mole ratio of H<sub>2</sub> to O<sub>2</sub>?
The theoretical yield of magnesium oxide is 120 g. Hana gets a yield of 70%. What mass does Hana collect?
Maya's calculation says 120 g of iron should form, but only 96 g is collected. What is the percent yield?
When magnesium burns: 2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO. You start with 6 mol of Mg and 2 mol of O<sub>2</sub>. Which is the limiting reactant?
items.e: The equation needs Mg : O<sub>2</sub> = 2 : 1; 6 mol Mg ÷ 2 = 3, 2 mol O<sub>2</sub> ÷ 1 = 2. The smaller one runs out first.

items.q: When magnesium reacts with acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>. You start with 12 mol of Mg and 10 mol of HCl. Which is the limiting reactant?
items.e: The equation needs Mg : HCl = 1 : 2; 12 mol Mg ÷ 1 = 12, 10 mol HCl ÷ 2 = 5. The smaller one runs out first.

items.q: 12.0 g of NaHCO<sub>3</sub> reacts completely: 2NaHCO<sub>3</sub> → Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub>. Calculate the maximum (theoretical) mass of Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>.
items.e: n(NaHCO3) = 0.143 mol, n(Na2CO3) = 0.0714 mol, m = 7.57 g.

items.q: 5.00 g of NaHCO<sub>3</sub> gave 1.42 g of Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (2NaHCO<sub>3</sub> → Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub>). Calculate the percentage yield.
The theoretical yield of magnesium oxide is 80 g. Nathan gets a yield of 80%. What mass does Nathan collect?

When propane burns in a grill: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O. You start with 12 mol of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> and 8 mol of O<sub>2</sub>. Which is the limiting reactant?
items.e: The equation needs C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> : O<sub>2</sub> = 1 : 5; 12 mol C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> ÷ 1 = 12, 8 mol O<sub>2</sub> ÷ 5 = 1.6. The smaller one runs out first.

items.q: Ava's calculation says 50 g of magnesium oxide should form, but only 42.5 g is collected. What is the percent yield?
The theoretical yield of magnesium oxide is 60 g. Emma gets a yield of 70%. What mass does Emma collect?
Calculate the percentage atom economy for making C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH by this reaction: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> → 2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 2CO<sub>2</sub>.
items.e: Atom economy = Mr of desired product ÷ total Mr of reactants × 100 = 92.00 ÷ 180.0 × 100 = 51.1%.

items.q: When hydrogen burns in oxygen: 2H<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2H<sub>2</sub>O. You start with 10 mol of H<sub>2</sub> and 2 mol of O<sub>2</sub>. How many moles of H<sub>2</sub>O can form?
items.e: O<sub>2</sub> is limiting; it gives 4 mol of H<sub>2</sub>O.

items.q: 50.0 g of N<sub>2</sub> gave 57.7 g of NH<sub>3</sub> (N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>). Calculate the percentage yield.
12.0 g of NaHCO<sub>3</sub> gave 7.19 g of Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (2NaHCO<sub>3</sub> → Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub>). Calculate the percentage yield.

25.0 g of C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> gave 7.67 g of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> → 2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 2CO<sub>2</sub>). Calculate the percentage yield.
The theoretical yield of aspirin is 200 g. Benjamin gets a yield of 90%. What mass does Benjamin collect?
25.0 mL of 0.050 mol/L Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> was neutralized by 21.4 mL of HCl. Calculate the concentration of the HCl.
items.e: n(Na2CO3) = 0.00125 mol; ratio acid : base = 1 : 1/2, so n(HCl) = 0.00250 mol; c = n/V = 0.117 mol/L.

items.q: Priya's calculation says 120 g of copper should form, but only 108 g is collected. What is the percent yield?
When iron rusts: 4Fe + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>. You start with 6 mol of Fe and 6 mol of O<sub>2</sub>. How many moles of Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> can form?
items.e: Fe is limiting; it gives 3 mol of Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.

items.q: When nitrogen oxide forms in an engine: N<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2NO. You start with 8 mol of N<sub>2</sub> and 5 mol of O<sub>2</sub>. Which is the limiting reactant?
items.e: The equation needs N<sub>2</sub> : O<sub>2</sub> = 1 : 1; 8 mol N<sub>2</sub> ÷ 1 = 8, 5 mol O<sub>2</sub> ÷ 1 = 5. The smaller one runs out first.
